title: System map source
description: The hand-written source of a product's system map (model.json). render_map.py checks a source against this file and renders the front page, the cards and the gaps list from it. Only points, bets, definitions and paths are written here; counts, each path's point, Touches and open work are derived at each render. A pointer to research or to a document goes in the `why` of the bet it supports; the map has no other place for one. A key that begins with x_ is the project's own and is ignored.

product.description: The product: the top of the tree.

frame.description: A short paragraph on how the product runs, shown above the diagram.

diagram.description: One simple architecture diagram as lines of plain text, drawn in a code block: the main parts and what flows between them.

bets.description: The product's bets, three to seven.

framework.description: The decision tree above the subjects.

angles.description: For software: Business logic, Interface, Infrastructure, QA. Otherwise three or four that split the product the same way, with QA kept; the tool flags a map with no angle named QA.

bets.description: Bets that hold for everything under this angle. May be empty.

areas.description: The angle's key areas: where a change is decided. Two to five is usual; the tool flags fewer than two. Write an area the sources name, empty or not; never add one only to quiet the flag.

subjects.description: Ids of the subjects decided here; may be empty until a later release. Every subject is in exactly one key area.

app.description: The Business logic subjects: the things users name. The tool flags an angle that holds both these and dimensions.

core.description: What users name that is not a module: the product's base records and the logic built on them. A record belongs to the logic subject it is about; how records are stored is an Infrastructure subject.

modules.description: Parts a customer can decline or switch off while the product's point still holds. Anything else users name is core.

dimensions.description: Parts of how the product is engineered: the Interface, Infrastructure and QA subjects, each answering one engineering question. With a dimension register, its questions; with none, start from the usual questions the method's dimensions page lists (`engineering-cycle-dimensions.md` beside the method; component.engineering_cycle_dimensions in Cady) and name one only where the product has code of its own for it. A quality (fast, secure) is not a subject.

loops.description: A loop is a flow that repeats and runs through several subjects, such as sign-up to first use, a sync or a release. Write the ones the sources name, when you list the subjects. May be empty.

nodes.description: Ids of the subjects it runs through, in order.

watch.description: Its known traps: what a source (an incident note, a code comment, a feedback document) says goes wrong. Never invent one.

items.description: One trap. It shows on the card of the subject that owns a cited file, or on every subject of the loop when no subject owns one.

when.description: The situation in which it goes wrong.

then.description: What goes wrong, and what to do about it when that is known.

releases.description: Ordered, the first current. A release is a goal a user can reach end to end, with the items that reach it. Take them from the tracker or roadmap; a dated list of work the owner asked for is a tracker: one release per list. With several lists, the current release is the list being worked now, or the newest dated one where the sources do not say, and comes first; the older lists follow, newest first, and an undated list comes last. An older list keeps only its open items: the map draws open items only, and the current release keeps its done ones as its record. An older list with none is left out, and one owner question names every list left out. An item is a piece of work a list asks for: group findings into the work that answers them, and do not copy every finding as an item. Where the tracker states no goal, write it and add an owner question to confirm it. With no tracker, write one release from the work the sources name (for a new product, the brief), leave `by` out and add an owner question to confirm its goal. When the sources name no work, leave the list empty and ask the owner.

by.description: Who set it and when. Leave out when unknown and ask the owner.

id.description: The item's id as the tracker writes it. Where the tracker has none, or repeats one, R<release number>.<item number> in build order, such as R1.2. No two items share one, in this release or another.

paths.description: The paths it changes or will create. It shows as open work on the card of each subject that owns one.

items.description: One file that needs two owners.

file.description: The file that needs two owners. The subject whose part stays in it owns it.

to.description: The path the moved part goes to: a home of the second subject, or inside one. It may not exist yet.

splits.description: The files this item separates: each needs two owners. A file needs two owners when a part of it belongs to another subject, by the method's Subjects paragraph and `home`: a top-level declaration, or a block that would be one once separated; a few lines inside a function do not count. Examples, not the whole list: logic with a screen, logic with a provider's calls, two logic subjects, two dimensions. A test file is placed by `home` and is not listed here. The map never gives such a file two owners; the fix is to separate it so each part has one. Unless the split is simple and reliable, change no code and write this item: open, in the current release, its `text` naming the file and the split, the file and the new path here, and both in `paths`. A migration or other shipped SQL, a generated or vendored file, and a path the project's instructions protect are always an item. A split is simple and reliable when whole top-level declarations move to a new file, no line inside them changes, elsewhere only import and export lines change, nothing but imports names the file by path (no manifest, bundle list, generated copy or mock), and a check you ran before and after would fail if a moved declaration were missing or wrongly linked: a test that runs the moved code or its caller, or the project's typecheck or build over every file whose imports changed; a test of the rest of the file does not count. Then split it now: make it as one commit of its own, before the map's commit, so either can be reverted alone; through the project's usual review, or where there is none leave it unmerged and undeployed and ask the owner to confirm it. The map keeps the item until that change has landed. The subject whose part stays in the file owns it; the second subject names the new path as a home, and one whose only code is the new path is written now, with that path planned. When the split has landed nothing changes owner: the second subject already names the new path, so set the item done and remove this key. The tool shows the file on the cards of both subjects, counts it, and refuses a row whose file no subject owns or whose new path is not a second subject's; a dimension that only governs the file is not the second owner.

status.description: next: not started, a decision still to make included. in progress: started, or built and not yet switched on. done: built and in the code, even when the release has not shipped. When sources disagree, the code decides; where the code cannot show it, take the less finished status and say the disagreement in `text`.

items.description: In build order, layer by layer: the first item not done is the next build step. A layer is what the next items read from: the stored shape, then the logic on it, then what reaches it.

questions.description: Questions only the owner can answer. One question covers like cases, such as every dimension's label. The gaps list shows at most seven, those that block the product's point, a release goal or a subject first, and says how many more there are.

blocks.description: What it blocks: product, a release id, or a subject id. Leave out when it blocks none of these.

id.description: An id: lower-case letters, digits, dot, underscore, colon or hyphen, starting with a letter or digit. No two angles, key areas, subjects, bets, loops, releases, items or questions share one.

path.description: A path inside the repository, relative to its root, as git lists it: no leading or trailing slash, no empty, `.` or `..` part, no tab, and no space at either end. A space inside a name is allowed.

bet.description: A choice that could have gone another way. One with no reason or no alternative stays and is counted as a gap; an owner's is counted on a line of its own, because only the owner can fill it.

The choice, as a statement. An owner bet is the owner's sentence, word for word. An owner sentence that states no choice goes into the point of the node it describes, in the owner's words where they fit.

instead_of.description: The option it replaced, when a source names it or plainly implies it. Otherwise leave it out: never invent one.

why.description: The recorded reason, when a source gives one. A research or document pointer goes here as file:<id> or file:<repository path>. For an unsigned statement, the quoted sentence. Where the research does not exist, say so here; the origin is still as `origin` says: inferred when a source shows the choice, proposed when none does.

origin.description: owner: a sentence the owner wrote, signed or said to you, or one in a document the owner gave you as theirs, such as the brief. inferred: what the code or a document implies, in your words, or a statement from a document that only sits in the repository and names no author, with the one sentence that states the choice quoted in `why`. proposed: your own choice, with nothing in the sources behind it; it is marked proposed and never written as decided. The owner is the person who decides the product. One owner question asks which of the unsigned documents are the owner's own and, where the sources name more than one person and do not say who decides, who the owner is; until it is answered those bets stay inferred.

source.description: Where the wording came from: the document and the place in it, such as brief.md, paragraph 2.

subject.description: A subject: something a person would change that has its own reason to exist. Not cut by folder or size: one file can be a subject, and so can a whole client; a folder that holds two subjects is split, each naming its files.

point.description: One sentence: why this subject exists. A dimension's point answers its one question.

bets.description: This subject's own choices. May be empty.

parts.description: The things inside the subject a reader would name, each with its point: its records, its main modules; for an Interface subject, its screens.

schema.description: The file that defines this part's shape, its fields and types: a table definition, a type file or a schema file. Where the shape is a folder of ordered migrations, name that folder. For a folder the tool checks only that it exists or that an item names it. The map points to it and never restates fields. While it is not written, an open item of the current release names this path itself and comes before the other open items of this subject. The tool checks that much; the order across subjects is the builder's to keep.

guarantees.description: What must stay true: a rule a source states or the code enforces. For code not yet built, write it now as the acceptance of the item that builds it. On the QA subject that holds the user journeys, if the product has one: one per journey goal with its acceptance (what the user sees when the goal is reached), in lifecycle order.

items.description: One thing that must stay true.

test.description: The test file that proves it. Leave out until the file exists and you have read that it proves the sentence.

home.description: The paths this subject owns, each a file or a folder. One subject owns a path. When paths nest, the longest matching path owns the file. A file belongs to the subject it is about. A client's Interface subject owns its screen and route code: code that reads or writes the page, a view or the address (the route); code that only returns markup or style text is not screen code. Reading browser storage or calling the API from a screen does not make a second owner; a file whose job is storage or the calls belongs to that dimension. A logic subject, or another dimension, names the client files that hold its rules. A file that needs two owners is not placed by a special rule: see an item's `splits`. On the server, a file that handles one subject's requests stays with that subject, its rules and handlers together; the Interface subject for the server's API owns the entry every request passes and lists the handler files under `governs`. It names its entry files one by one, because the tool refuses a governed path inside the dimension's own home. A subject names its own test files inside a shared test folder, and a build script belongs to the subject whose code it builds; the rest of the shared tests, with CI scripts, stays with the QA subject that runs them. A document belongs to the subject it is about; one about several subjects, the brief included, belongs to no subject. The README, agent instruction files, package and ignore files and the map's own folder belong to no subject: unowned files are expected. A path that does not exist yet must be named by an item of the current release. A path that states no point renders "no point stated": leave the map so; the fix is the file's own first line, in the project's own change.

tools.description: Commands or callable operations defined in this subject's own code: a script the package file names, a CLI command, a served operation. A build script is listed on the subject whose code it builds, which also owns its file. The tool does not find these; list them when you list the subject.

name.description: The command as typed, or the operation's name.

dimension.description: A dimension subject: a part of how the product is engineered that answers one question.

point.description: One sentence: why this subject exists. A dimension's point answers its one question.

bets.description: This subject's own choices. May be empty. With a dimension register, the first is its label: differentiating or not, with the reason. With no register, leave out the label, the register ids and the owner, and ask for every dimension's label in one owner question; a technology choice the sources already show is still written, as an inferred bet.

parts.description: The things inside the subject a reader would name, each with its point: its records, its main modules; for an Interface subject, its screens.

schema.description: The file that defines this part's shape, its fields and types: a table definition, a type file or a schema file. The tool checks that much; the order across subjects is the builder's to keep.

On the QA subject that holds the user journeys, if the product has one: one per journey goal with its acceptance (what the user sees when the goal is reached), in lifecycle order.

governs.description: Paths another subject owns whose rules this dimension sets, such as the checks every route passes, or the handler files behind the server's API entry; never a path inside its own home. The dimension owns none of them: each shows on this card as governed, the owning card names this dimension, and its open work and traps show on both.

A build script is listed on the subject whose code it builds, which also owns its file. The tool does not find these; list them when you list the subject.

name.description: The command as typed, or the operation's name.

register_ids.description: Its rows in the dimension register, where one exists.

owner.description: Its one owner, copied from the dimension register, where one exists.
